speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Some months ago, the BBC Global Survey found that three in four people around the world thought their country was divided, and six in 10 felt their country was more divided now than it was 10 years ago.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With the prevalence of identity politics, many countries today find themselves fractured along partisan lines, or struggling to bring communities across racial and socio-economic divides together.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, I am heartened to see that over the last 10 days, Members of this House were unified by the common goal of creating a better future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In 2017, this Parliament set its teeth on economic transformation; last year, we tackled social inequality.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This year, Members seized recent developments in our geopolitical and digital world with the high number of questions received by the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI), Ministry of Defence (MINDEF), Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) and Ministry of Health (MOH) on our diplomatic relations, physical security as well as cybersecurity.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The social Ministries also received a record high number of cuts, as significant emphasis was placed on educating and training Singaporeans for the future, and caring for the aged and the vulnerable.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MCCY received the highest number of cuts and longest “cut” time, reflecting Members’ interest in volunteerism, art and culture, and community relations.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have had robust debates over the past weeks.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I observe that Members agreed on three key things.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, that we need to put Singaporeans at the heart of our policies.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A good many Members stressed that in pursuing economic progress, we must not leave our workers behind.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Denise Phua, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Dr Intan Mokhtar reminded us that our workforce needs to be an inclusive one, as those with special needs and those advanced in their years also have much to offer, and ought to be treated with dignity.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan and Prof Lim Sun Sun talked about improving the working environment for women.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Putting Singaporeans at the centre of what we do extends also to the social sector.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: My Ministry has made it its focus to ensure that Singaporeans from all walks of life can engage in sports and enjoy the arts.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) talked about what it will do to ensure that every Singaporean has a strong foundation in education, starting from preschool.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, Members agreed that while we work on the present, we must keep an eye on the future.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Pritam Singh pointed out that we must leverage technology to ensure that critical functions, like national security, are not affected by our shrinking population.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry and MCI spoke about how we must focus on innovation and creativity and help our businesses digitalise to ensure our competitiveness in the future economy and that the purpose of future-proofing our economy is so that our workers will seize the new opportunities that the future will bring.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We were also reminded that we must maintain fiscal prudence so that we do not burden our future generations with our decisions today, and that we must find the next water story in waste and food and be responsible towards our environment, even as the effects of climate change will be felt in decades to come.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: That we are thinking far into the future, planning for the future and acting for the future now is the hallmark of Singapore.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: How do we know if the long-term plans we make are going in the right direction?

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The answer lies in the third theme that has run through this debate.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By giving space for civic participation and partnerships in our policies and implementation of plans, we can forge effective solutions, leverage one another’s expertise and strengths, and do good by all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Several Ministries are conducting public consultations so that the Government and the people can co-develop effective solutions.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through the Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers, the Government gathered feedback from workers, employers, union leaders and other stakeholders to inform policies to support older workers.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development, MCCY and MOH are building an extensive network of community support and volunteers to care for the elderly and uplift low-income families.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To ground our work in designing housing and facilities for assisted living, the Ministry of National Development and MOH will be consulting senior citizens and healthcare providers.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ministries are also working more closely with one another.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To use the words of Prof Lim Sun Sun, this has been a forum where we are unafraid of asking tough questions of one another.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They have researched, studied and presented their case with robustness.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On behalf of the House, I would also like to thank you, Mr Speaker, and your deputies for your stewardship.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are also grateful to the Parliament Secretariat and all those who have helped behind the scenes, including the interpreters, for providing their steadfast support.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I spent the last year – it is a very long year – thinking about what to say today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I was actually quite tempted to repeat the same speech from last year, not because you would not notice it, because I am sure you paid rapt attention to it last year, but also because some fundamentals actually do not change.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: At the heart of everything we do, and we have heard that, it is that it surely must be about Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But as we all know, what is ideal for the individual is not always optimal for society, for Singapore as a whole.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: What is best for Singapore, as a whole, may not always be maximal for the individual.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And if you add in the perspective of time, there are urgent needs of today and there are also contingencies of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are our pressing wants and desires that are here and now, but there are also those of our children and our children’s children in the many, many years to come.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If we are an inherently selfish society, we will only be preoccupied with the individual and the present.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Is this who we are and what we aspire to be?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When we look around the world, some systems are running from pillar to post, from one election cycle to another because the preoccupation is the present, just to get elected.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Some systems operate in ways not because the work they do makes sense but how it makes dollars and cents for them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Long-term investments in public infrastructure are not always made because you do not reap the political dividends of these efforts.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: By the time the projects are ready, someone else will be benefiting from your generosity.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The monies are better spent on initiatives where people respond to, in the way they vote, today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In countries where the systems are corrupt, you will actually initiate these projects, in fact, many projects, because that is where you cream off the kickbacks, and you make what you can because sometimes you do not know how long you are going to be there.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These projects are seldom seen all the way through.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Either way, there is precious little long-term planning to talk about.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because it is always about me and it is always about the present.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Is there, as Minister Heng Swee Keat puts it, a "Singapore way" where we are actually interested in others and not just self, and where we are actually interested in our future and not just the present?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Otto von Bismarck said, "Politics is the art of the possible, the attainable – the art of the next best." That is where we come in.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These are the blueprints we lay down, and the difficult choices we make here during the Budget to attain the possible.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To do this well, we need to have perspective.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We need to have a sense of history, a sense of time and space, where we came from, why and how our story and policies have evolved.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We need to know the context and how it and the world are changing.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As we debate this Budget and all its details, we need to remember that this Budget is built upon what has been said by many of you and in the years past and also based on inputs surfaced by our fellow Singaporeans in many, many different forums.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Budgets are built upon Budgets of years gone by.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There is always a context and there is always a system in place.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Actually, a simple search online will yield you an existing menu of universal benefits and schemes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When we begin to understand the context of each group that we are looking at, you then realise that there are differentiated needs as well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Hence, you layer it on with various packages.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There will be those who feel that they are not directly benefiting from the Budget, but it is useful to remember, and we have been through the debates in the last two weeks, that we have honoured so many different groups, but it is also useful for us to cast our eyes back to previous Budgets, where it is clear that we have also benefited in different ways.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In this COS, the well-being of one particular animal was at stake.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many supported the slaughtering of this particular sacred cow, including, surprisingly, Mr Louis Ng.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It sounds exciting but it may be disastrous if we do not understand why the cow was put out to pasture in the first place.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: While every cow is a good cow, no cow is perfect.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because over the years, we have learnt that it emits methane gas so, therefore, it impacts the environment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, over the years, as he has shared, we have sought to trim the cow, adjust its diet, sliced off its rump, have a little barbeque, its flanks, and finally, we lay it to rest.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is a far less dramatic story, but I think a more accurate one and a recognition of the work done by many to get to where we are today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I know that the slaying of sacred cows sounds bold, it sounds daring, even romantic, perhaps.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But I think it is useful for us to also remember, with a sense of perspective, that that is not the objective.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, even as we make bold moves, never do it for its own sake.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Some have asked if the various Budget goodies are part of a cynical election scheme.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, having a perspective of how the system works may help us understand why some of these major initiatives can be launched at this stage.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And let us also begin to have a sense of reality and see how the world operates elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will shift the burden to the future.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because the monies can be spent to make all of us happier in so many different ways.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is actually incredibly politically naïve to do so!

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Which government in the world would embark on this when they have funds and reserves to do so many more things to keep the electorate happy?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But that is not the way we are.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And I do not just mean the Government but I would like to also highlight that the Opposition, at least this Opposition presently in the House, and our NMPs over the years, in spite of occasional differences and disagreements over details, we support this approach and do not just seek wanton political largesse and populism.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But we can only do this, we can only take this approach if – and only if – our fellow Singaporeans support it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This can only happen if they also understand the issues that are grappled with and debated here and have that same sense of perspective.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But do Singaporeans take reference from what is articulated here or from other sources?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are we Singaporeans very evidence-based in the way we look at things?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When that happens, you lose the mandate and space to make the difficult decisions for the long haul and the greater good even as you endeavour to make life better for individuals today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When that happens, there will be a reversion to the norm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And the norm is an absence of long-term planning.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And what will Singapore look like then when that does not exist?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In my inaugural speech in Parliament, I said that we, Parliament, need to be a beacon from where Singaporeans can take reference, with confidence, when addressing and understanding issues that will matter greatly for our collective well-being.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To be this beacon and to do this well, we need to gain the trust and respect of the public.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In the past two weeks, if we actually listen to the points made by the ruling party, the Opposition, the NMPs, the front bench, we will find that different perspectives are shared and articulated.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have an Opposition that does not shy away from making sharp challenges.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Notwithstanding the fact that there is no tussle over balloons this year, whether trial balloons or otherwise, you will find Members of Parliament on both sides of the House pushing and pointing out issues that may not sit comfortably with the Government.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will, therefore, be able to put people and our society at the centre of everything that we do; plan for the present as well as the long term, and grapple with all the difficult challenges and tradeoffs that need to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: While we may not have the same mudflats to metropolis transformation on the same scale on many fronts, we can continually improve, and we will, and extend our edge so that we can better provide for our people.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But we can have a mudflat to metropolis transformation in the kind of people we want to be, and the society we can be.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Irene Quay's sharing and story on the volunteering journey is inspiring and is exactly what SG Cares is all about.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As we begin to volunteer, as we begin to lose ourselves in the service of others, we will begin to change, and we will find ourselves as a society where we care not just about self, but about others, and also about the future.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The wonderful thing about it is that it actually does not cost us very much, except a bit of organisation and a bit of our time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And it is something that every one of us here, and every Singaporean can do something about.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When we become that kind of society, then I would say that we will live long and prosper, and that our best years are truly, truly ahead of us.
